doc.title: Marian McPartland interviewed by Monk Rowe, Utica, New York, April 26, 1997

title: Women's jazz festivals and women in the business
summary: Women's festivals in Kansas City and Billy Taylor's tribute, and the growing number of women in media jobs.

story.theme_name: Late-career reflections: awards, legacy and life lessons
story.community_name: Politics, race and the state of the country

blocks.x: I suppose in a perfect world it might not be necessary to have — I was just reading the other day that I think in two weekends there will be a women’s jazz festival in Washington I think it is. So maybe, as I said in a perfect world it wouldn’t be necessary to have a “women’s” jazz festival, but they would just have a jazz festival there would be a proportional amount of women players.

Well we always said this, like when they had the Kansas City women’s festival, that was a long time ago, I think you were probably a real young boy then — I can’t remember how long ago, gee maybe it’s 15 or 20 years — and this was the, like the biggest jazz festival ever. Mary Lou Williams played it and I played it and Toshiko Akiyoshi had her big band, and I mean it was a large event. And they carried that on for three or four years and then they ran out of money. So actually, what Billy Taylor is doing, it’s the same kind of thing. They had it last year but they called it “A Tribute to Mary Lou Williams,” which was fine. And I was in it and the Maria Schneider big band and Joanne Brackeen. And I mean they certainly didn’t have to wont for good women players. Jane Ira Bloom, a wonderful sax player, so I don’t exactly know the cast of characters for this year but some of them — Trudy Pitts, a good piano player, I can’t remember, they had Maria Schneider’s big band again and there’s another woman’s big band called Diva, very, very good. But it’s true, I mean you don’t ever have to say Woody Herman and his all-male band, but yet you do have to say Diva is an all-girl band. It’s still a novelty and maybe it always will be I don’t know.
It’s almost the same in sports you know. They’re trying so hard to have professional women’s basketball for instance and it’s an uphill battle I guess.

Well I mean for everything. I remember years ago like doing T.V. shows, now you never, ever saw a woman cameraperson, or a women being an assistant producer or a producer. Whereas like now, my producer for “Piano Jazz” is a woman, and my manager is a woman, and my publicist is a woman, you know and I’m thinking gee, what’s going on I’m surrounded by all these chicks, I would like to get away from this. What happened to the guys? If they hear me I’m not serious.
